summary:
Lunar Vista is a scientific exploration tool that helps users compare candidate lunar south pole sites by investigating when the Sun is available for power generation and when Earth is visible for direct-to-Earth communication.

The project combines NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data with JPL DE440 ephemerides and NASA SPICE kernels. Its Python engine calculates the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth relative to selected lunar sites, while a terrain-horizon model accounts for lunar curvature and surrounding topography. The web application presents site-specific visibility metrics across different observer heights and time periods.

Lunar Vista makes complex orbital and terrain calculations accessible through an interactive browser, helping users explore how local topography affects illumination and communication opportunities for future lunar missions.

The current model has passed several numerical and cross-check tests. Far-field terrain effects and published site rankings remain under investigation, so its results are exploratory rather than mission-certified predictions.
details:
Purpose

Lunar Vista explores two important constraints on lunar surface operations: sunlight availability for power and direct visibility of Earth for communication. These conditions are strongly influenced by the Moon's terrain and changing celestial geometry.

How it works

The Python engine uses NASA SPICE kernels and the JPL DE440 planetary ephemeris to calculate the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth in a Moon-fixed reference frame. It transforms these positions into local azimuth and elevation coordinates for seven candidate locations near the lunar south pole.

For each location, the terrain engine casts rays along 360 azimuth directions through NASA PGDA/LRO LOLA elevation tiles. It calculates the highest terrain angle in each direction while accounting for lunar curvature. Visibility metrics include the percentage of time a celestial body's centre or any part of its apparent disk is visible, the longest continuous illumination period, and the longest darkness interval.

The Python engine exports site data to JSON, which the web application uses to display and compare locations, dates, and observer heights of 2, 5, 10, and 20 metres.

Benefits and intended impact

Lunar Vista helps users investigate how terrain, observer height, and celestial motion affect potential solar-power and communication opportunities. It provides an accessible starting point for comparing candidate exploration locations and understanding the environmental constraints of future lunar missions.

Technology

Python, NumPy, SpiceyPy, Rasterio, Skyfield, JavaScript-based web technologies, NASA SPICE kernels, and NASA PGDA/LRO LOLA elevation data.

Validation and limitations

The project includes synthetic-terrain tests, checks of astronomical geometry, and a SPICE pipeline cross-check against Skyfield. However, local terrain tiles do not capture distant obstructions beyond their boundaries. Far-field terrain validation and published site-ranking comparisons remain open. Results are therefore intended for exploration and comparison, not as certified operational predictions.
